steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening at dusk, Margaret climbed the 112 steps.

She had counted them the first week after her husband died, needing something to count, something reliable. One hundred and twelve. They never changed. The Atlantic beneath them, however, changed constantly — green one morning, black the next, silver when the moon hit it right and made the whole ocean look like something worth swimming into.

She had taken the job because nobody else wanted it. The island was three miles offshore, accessible by supply boat twice a month. There was no grocery store, no church, no neighbor to wave at from across a fence. There was the cottage, the tower, the light, and the sea.

People in town called it lonely work. Margaret called it honest work.

She learned the birds first. Then the tides. Then she learned to read the particular shade of green the water turned before a storm rolled in — deeper than usual, almost bruised. She would light the lamp early on those nights, giving the fishermen extra time to read her warning.

She saved eleven lives over fourteen years. She knew this because she kept a journal, and the coast guard kept records, and sometimes the fishermen came out on the supply boat just to shake her hand, sunburned men with calloused palms who looked at her the way people look at someone they cannot quite explain.

One January, a young man arrived — a journalist from the mainland wanting to write about isolation, about what solitude does to the human mind.

"Don't you miss people?" he asked, his recorder held out like an offering.

Margaret watched the light make its slow rotation above them.

"I see a ship's light most nights," she said. "Someone out there, going somewhere. That's enough."

He wrote his article. He described her as lonely.

She read it on the supply boat, laughed once, and climbed her 112 steps.

The lamp was waiting. The sea was waiting.

She lit the light.
